lessons.title: Personal protective equipment (PPE) for cutting, lifting, and chemical handling
lessons.body:
In a scrapyard, your body is your most valuable tool. Without proper PPE, you risk cuts, burns, eye injuries, and lung damage. Start with the basics: steel-toe boots with puncture-resistant soles (around $30-50) protect your feet from falling metal and nails. Leather gloves are essential for handling sharp parts, but for cutting and welding, use flame-resistant gloves like Kevlar or leather. Never wear synthetic gloves near heatâthey melt into skin.

For eye and face protection, always wear safety glasses with side shields under a face shield when grinding or cutting. A full-face shield (about $15) stops sparks and metal shards. When using torches, a welding helmet with at least a #10 shade lens prevents arc eye and burns. Ear protectionâearplugs or earmuffsâis critical when using impact wrenches, grinders, or hammers; noise above 85 dB can cause permanent hearing loss.

For chemical handling (battery acid, solvents, antifreeze), wear chemical-resistant gloves (nitrile or neoprene), goggles, and a face shield. A PVC apron or coveralls protect your clothes and skin. When draining fuel or oil, use nitrile glovesâthey resist hydrocarbons. For battery work, add a rubber apron and acid-resistant boots. Always have a respirator with organic vapor cartridges (like 3M 6001) when working with solvents or in enclosed spaces. Dust masks (N95) are for grinding dust, but they don't stop vapors.

Inspect your PPE daily. Replace cracked goggles, torn gloves, or worn boots. Keep spare PPE in a clean, dry place. In hot African climates, choose lightweight, breathable optionsâlike ventilated hard hats and moisture-wicking coverallsâto prevent heat stress. Remember: PPE only works if you wear it correctly and consistently. Train your team to check each other before starting work.

lessons.title: Safe lifting techniques and use of engine hoists and jacks
lessons.body:
Lifting heavy engine blocks, transmissions, or scrap metal by hand is a leading cause of back injuries in scrapyards. Always assess the load: if it's over 25 kg (55 lbs), use mechanical aid. For anything over 50 kg, use a hoist or get a partner. The correct lifting technique: stand close to the load, feet shoulder-width apart, bend your knees (not your back), keep the load close to your body, and lift smoothly by straightening your legs. Never twist while liftingâturn your whole body by moving your feet.

Engine hoists (cherry pickers) are essential for pulling engines. Before use, check the hydraulic jack for leaks, the chain for wear, and the legs for cracks. Position the hoist so the arm is directly over the load. Attach the chain to the engine's lifting eyes or use a load leveler. Raise slowly, keeping everyone clear. Never exceed the hoist's rated capacity (typically 1-2 tons). Lower the load slowly and set it on blocksânever leave it suspended.

For jacks, use a trolley jack (floor jack) with a minimum 2-ton capacity for cars. Place it under the frame or axle, not the floor pan. Always use jack standsânever rely on a jack alone. Set the stands on firm, level ground. For scrapyard work, a bottle jack is handy for lifting heavy parts. Check the oil level and seals before use. When lifting a vehicle, chock the wheels and apply the parking brake.

In Africa, many scrapyards use makeshift methods like ropes and poles. Avoid theseâthey cause crush injuries. Invest in a good hoist and jack stands; they pay for themselves in safety. Train workers to communicate clearly during lifting: use hand signals or a spotter. Never walk under a suspended load. Store hoists and jacks in a dry place to prevent rust.

lessons.title: Fire prevention and control when using torches and grinders
lessons.body:
Torches and grinders create sparks that can ignite fuel, oil, and dry vegetation. Before cutting or grinding, clear the area of flammable materials within 10 meters (30 feet). Remove rags, paper, and plastic. If working on a vehicle, drain fuel and oil first, or at least ensure no leaks. Keep a fire extinguisher (dry chemical, ABC rated) within reachâat least 5 kg. Also have a bucket of sand or water nearby. Never use water on electrical fires or fuel fires; use foam or dry powder.

When using an oxy-acetylene torch, check hoses for cracks and connections for leaks with soapy water. Light the torch with a striker, not a lighter. Keep the flame away from hoses and cylinders. Store cylinders upright, secured with chains, and away from heat. Never lay acetylene cylinders on their side. When grinding, direct sparks away from yourself and others. Use a spark guard or a welding blanket to contain sparks. Wear leather apron and sleevesâsynthetic clothing melts and sticks to skin.

In hot, dry African conditions, grass fires are a real risk. Keep the work area clear of dry grass and have a fire watch during and after hot work for at least 30 minutes. If a fire starts, stay calm. For small fires, use the extinguisher: pull the pin, aim at the base, squeeze, and sweep. For larger fires, evacuate and call for help. Never turn your back on a fire.

Maintain your equipment: replace worn grinding discs, check torch tips for damage, and keep hoses away from sharp edges. Train everyone on the PASS method (Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep). Conduct monthly fire drills. Remember, prevention is cheaper than fire damageâinvest in fire blankets and extinguishers, and enforce a no-smoking policy near fuel areas.

lessons.title: Managing oil, fuel, and chemical spills to protect the environment
lessons.body:
Spills in a scrapyard contaminate soil and groundwater, harming your community and violating environmental laws. Prevent spills by using drip trays under vehicles, funnels when pouring, and secure lids on containers. Store oil, fuel, and chemicals in labeled, leak-proof containers on a concrete pad with a bund (a raised edge) to contain spills. Never store chemicals near drains or water sources.

If a spill happens, act fast. For small oil spills (under 5 liters), use absorbent materials like sawdust, sand, or commercial absorbent pads. Sprinkle around the spill, work inward, and sweep up. For fuel, use a spill kit with pads and socks. Never wash spills into drainsâthat pollutes rivers. For battery acid, neutralize with baking soda or lime, then absorb with sand. Wear PPE: nitrile gloves, goggles, and apron.

For larger spills (over 20 liters), contain the spread with sandbags or booms, then call local environmental authorities if it reaches water. Collect used absorbents in sealed bags and dispose of as hazardous waste. Clean the area with detergent and water, but capture the runoff. In Africa, many scrapyards lack proper drainageâdig a temporary pit lined with plastic to contain runoff.

Prevention is key: inspect vehicles for leaks before dismantling, use a funnel, and train workers to report spills immediately. Keep a spill kit stocked with absorbents, gloves, goggles, and bags. Post emergency numbers for fire and environmental agencies. Remember, a clean scrapyard is a safe and profitable oneâoil can be recycled, and a good reputation attracts customers.

lessons.title: Proper disposal of hazardous waste: batteries, tires, and fluids
lessons.body:
Hazardous waste from car breaking includes lead-acid batteries, tires, and fluids like oil, antifreeze, and brake fluid. These cannot go to regular landfills. Batteries contain lead and sulfuric acidârecycle them at a licensed facility. In many African countries, battery recyclers pay for used batteries. Store them upright in a leak-proof container, away from children and animals. Never break batteries open; the acid burns skin and eyes.

Tires are a fire hazard and breeding ground for mosquitoes. They cannot be burnedâburning releases toxic fumes. Instead, sell tires for retreading or use them for erosion control, playgrounds, or artificial reefs (check local regulations). Many scrapyards stockpile tires for recycling into crumb rubber. Store tires in a covered area to prevent water collection.

Fluids: Drain all fluids before dismantling. Use separate containers for oil, coolant, and fuelânever mix. Oil can be recycled into fuel or re-refined. Antifreeze (ethylene glycol) is highly toxicâstore in labeled containers and recycle. Brake fluid is also toxic. Never pour fluids on the ground or into drains. Use a funnel and drip trays. For small amounts, absorb with sawdust and dispose as hazardous waste.

Find local recyclers: contact your city council or environmental agency for licensed hazardous waste handlers. In Kenya, for example, the National Environment Management Authority (NEMA) licenses handlers. Keep records of disposalâthis proves compliance. Train workers to identify hazardous waste and never burn or bury it. Proper disposal protects your health, your community, and your business from fines.

lessons.title: First aid for cuts, burns, and chemical exposure in the scrapyard
lessons.body:
In a scrapyard, injuries happen fast. For cuts, stop bleeding by applying direct pressure with a clean cloth or sterile gauze. Elevate the wound above the heart. Once bleeding slows, clean with clean water and mild soap. Apply antibiotic ointment and cover with a sterile bandage. If the cut is deep, gaping, or won't stop bleeding, get medical help. For puncture wounds (like from nails), check for embedded objectsâdo not remove them; seek medical care. Ensure tetanus shots are up to date.

For burns, cool the burn under running water for at least 10 minutesânot ice. Remove jewelry or clothing near the burn, but don't peel off stuck fabric. Cover with a sterile, non-stick dressing. For chemical burns, flush with plenty of water for 20 minutes. For acid burns from batteries, flush with water, then apply a paste of baking soda and water. For alkali burns (like from lye), flush with water and vinegar. Never use ointments on severe burns. Seek medical help for burns larger than a palm, or on face, hands, or joints.

Chemical exposure: If a chemical splashes in the eyes, flush with clean water for 15-20 minutes, holding eyelids open. Remove contact lenses if present. For skin contact, remove contaminated clothing and wash with soap and water. If fumes are inhaled, move to fresh air and loosen tight clothing. If swallowed, do not induce vomitingâcall poison control or a doctor immediately. Keep a first aid kit stocked with bandages, gauze, antiseptic, burn gel, eye wash, and activated charcoal. Post emergency numbers. Train all workers in basic first aid and CPR. In remote areas, have a plan to transport injured workers to a clinic quickly.

quiz.q: What type of gloves should you wear when using a torch or grinder?
quiz.explanation: Leather or flame-resistant gloves protect against heat and sparks, while synthetic gloves can melt.

quiz.q: When lifting a heavy engine block by hand, you should:
options: A) Bend your back and lift quickly
B) Keep the load away from your body
C) Bend your knees and keep the load close
D) Twist your body while lifting
quiz.explanation: Bending knees and keeping the load close reduces strain on your back.

quiz.q: What is the minimum weight above which you should use mechanical aid for lifting?
quiz.explanation: Lifting over 25 kg by hand increases risk of injury; use a hoist or partner.

quiz.q: Before using an engine hoist, you should check:
options: A) The color of the paint
B) Hydraulic jack for leaks and chain for wear
quiz.explanation: Leaks and worn chains can cause sudden failure and dropping of the load.

quiz.q: When using a jack to lift a vehicle, you must always:
options: A) Rely on the jack alone
C) Place it under the floor pan
quiz.explanation: Jack stands provide stable support; jacks can fail.

quiz.q: What should you do before cutting or grinding on a vehicle?
quiz.explanation: Fuel and oil are flammable; draining them prevents fires.

quiz.q: Which fire extinguisher is suitable for fuel fires?
quiz.explanation: ABC dry chemical extinguishers are effective on fuel, electrical, and ordinary fires.

quiz.q: How far should flammable materials be cleared from hot work?
quiz.explanation: A 10-meter clearance prevents sparks from igniting nearby materials.

quiz.q: When lighting an oxy-acetylene torch, you should use:
quiz.explanation: A striker is safe and designed for torches; lighters can explode.

quiz.q: After hot work, you should maintain a fire watch for at least:
quiz.explanation: Smoldering fires can start after you leave; 30 minutes ensures safety.

quiz.q: What is the first step when a small oil spill occurs?
options: A) Wash it into a drain
quiz.explanation: Absorbents like sawdust or pads contain the spill and prevent spreading.

quiz.q: How should you neutralize a battery acid spill?
options: B) With baking soda or lime
quiz.explanation: Baking soda or lime neutralizes acid safely.

quiz.q: Where should you store oil and chemicals?
options: B) On a concrete pad with bund
quiz.explanation: A bund contains leaks and prevents environmental contamination.

quiz.q: What should you do with used absorbents from a spill?
quiz.explanation: Absorbents contaminated with oil or chemicals are hazardous waste.

quiz.q: Why should you never burn tires?
options: A) They are too hard to burn
quiz.explanation: Burning tires releases harmful chemicals and pollutants.

quiz.q: How should lead-acid batteries be disposed of?
quiz.explanation: Batteries contain lead and acid; recycling prevents pollution.

quiz.q: Why should you never mix different fluids like oil and antifreeze?
options: B) They become harder to recycle
quiz.explanation: Mixing fluids complicates recycling and may create hazardous reactions.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to store tires?
quiz.explanation: Covered storage prevents water collection and mosquito breeding.

quiz.q: For a deep cut that won't stop bleeding, you should:
options: B) Apply direct pressure and seek medical help
quiz.explanation: Direct pressure controls bleeding; deep cuts need professional care.

quiz.q: How long should you cool a burn under running water?
quiz.explanation: Cooling for at least 10 minutes reduces tissue damage.

quiz.q: If battery acid splashes in your eye, you should:
options: B) Flush with water for 15-20 minutes
D) Close your eye and rest
quiz.explanation: Flushing removes acid and prevents further damage.

quiz.q: What should you do if someone inhales chemical fumes?
options: B) Move them to fresh air
quiz.explanation: Fresh air helps clear fumes from the lungs.

quiz.q: What is included in a basic first aid kit for a scrapyard?
quiz.explanation: Bandages, gauze, and antiseptic treat common cuts and burns.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep tetanus shots up to date?
options: A) Tetanus is caused by rust
B) Tetanus bacteria live in soil and can enter cuts
quiz.explanation: Tetanus bacteria are common in soil and can infect puncture wounds.

quiz.q: What PPE is essential when handling battery acid?
options: B) Rubber apron and acid-resistant boots
quiz.explanation: Rubber apron and acid-resistant boots protect against corrosive acid.

quiz.q: When using a grinder, you should direct sparks:
options: B) Away from yourself and others
quiz.explanation: Directing sparks away prevents burns and fires.

quiz.q: What is the PASS method for fire extinguishers?
quiz.explanation: PASS is the standard technique for using a fire extinguisher.

quiz.q: Why should you never use water on an electrical fire?
quiz.explanation: Water conducts electricity and can cause electrocution.

quiz.q: What is a bund?
options: B) A raised edge to contain spills
quiz.explanation: A bund is a containment barrier around storage areas.

quiz.q: How can you prevent spills when draining fluids?
options: A) Use a funnel and drip trays
C) Use a bucket with holes
quiz.explanation: Funnels and drip trays capture fluids and prevent spills.
